blocks.x: I'll make a note on here first that we're interviewing Johnny Wiggs out at his home
on Betts Place. What is the number? 345 Betts Place at 238 DuPlessis Street. Take your pick.
And the date is Sunday August the 26th 1962 and this is Bill Russell doing the interviewing or trying to. Do you want to give your full name Johnny that you were born with? John Wigington Hyman.

The Wigington is W-I-G-G-I-N-T-O-N and the hyman is H-Y-M-A-N. Do you mind giving the exact date that you were born and where exactly? July the 25th 1899 1700 block Louisiana Avenue in New Orleans. I'm almost sure it was a 1700 block. Where is that? Is that near between St. Charles and Ferret? No, it's a block and two doors off of St. Charles. One block and two doors off of St. Charles. In other words in the second block off St. Charles going towards the lake.
Can you tell us anything about your childhood, your background, your family in particular? Anybody play music? Can you, your father or mother, any of them musicians or sing?

Yeah, my mother played piano by ear and sang and I don't know whether my father played any musical instruments or not. I don't think he did but he sang and he had a talent for music. You had a piano in the home then? Yeah, we had a piano in the home, yeah.

Can you tell anything about the earliest music you remember hearing when you were a kid? Even three or four years old or anything like that? What it was like? Even if it wasn't a band, anything singing in your home?

I can't remember anything definite except that I seemed to have in the back of my mind somewhere this sound of colored women over washing on wash days. You know, the singing with their rough voices, their beautiful roughness, you know, I don't mean a disagreeable word when I say rough. There's a certain beauty in it to me in that voice. One of the nicest things that I know, really, in that particular kind of voice. And I seem to remember an awful lot of that when I was young. And then later on, when I was, must have been around seven or eight years old, of course, something that sticks in my mind, I've spoken to you often about, is the bottle man. We were living on Henry Clay Avenue then. 711 Henry Clay Avenue. 711, how do you like that? Maybe that isn't a number, but it's... Where is that exactly? No, I beg your pardon, it wasn't 711, it was 1115. 1115 Henry Clay Avenue. But we did live in the 700 block of Henry Clay Avenue. And then we moved later to 1115.
Where is Henry Clay? What streets are next to it about?

Henry Clay is two blocks from Audubon Park. Henry Clay and then Calhoun and then Audubon Park. Oh yeah. Oh yeah, sure. It's up in the uptown section. Yeah. And this house was near the, what was then called the Louisiana Retreat. It was a place for insane people. Oh. Uh, what is it called now? Up up at the Magazine Street about? Yeah, it's in between Magazine and uh... St. Charles? Uh, Paria. In between Magazine and Paria. I don't know whether it runs... No, it doesn't run quite to Magazine. It's a couple blocks, starts a couple blocks away from Magazine. Yeah. Uh, Batty? Batty? Batty? Want to turn it off? Yeah. No, what is the name, what do they call the Louisiana, uh... Louisiana Retreat. Oh yeah, they call it DePaul, uh... What? DePaul Sanitarium now? Oh no. It's still a retreat for uh, uh, insane people. Yeah. And left the new one. Anyway. And uh, then of course, uh, LaSalle School that I went to when I was a child was uh, one block downtown. In the same... Was that a public school or... Yeah, it was a public school, yeah. Mm-hmm. And oh, I wanted to tell you about uh, when I was around seven, uh, I wanted to tell you about the Bottle Man. Oh yeah. One of the, one of the most uh, uh, influential things I believe uh, uh, uh, in uh, my musical department in my life.
What kind of a wagon or what did they... Was the only wagon?

Well, the Bottle Man collected uh, uh, bottles uh, as the uh, title indicates. Uh, and he went around uh, uh, blowing on his horn. And he'd give uh, uh, uh, little prize, little uh, uh, dolls and uh, and uh, pieces of furniture and uh, candy if you wanted it. He had various uh, uh, souvenirs to give you in trade for the bottles. So of course the kids would go in the back shed and collect all the bottles and then... What kind of were they soft drink? Well, he'd uh, you'd, you'd bring out all the bottles you had and then he'd pick out the ones he wanted and uh, leave the others with you. The ones that he didn't want. Of course he wanted mostly uh, uh, I think, I imagine, those expensive seltzer bottles, you know. Oh yeah. And uh, uh, the better of the bottles. The better bottles I had, I imagine he would uh, collect. Well, anyway, uh, coming down the street, he had a uh, he had a horn that he blew on. Now this horn was uh, was a regular noise making horn of that day, a carnival noise making horn, uh, uh, Christmas, uh, New Year's Eve noise making horn. But in those days, uh, of course everything was made better uh, than they make them now. They make things, you know, just, especially if it's a souvenir horn, carnival horn, lucky if it lasts out the night. But in those days, uh, Payne's uh,
Have a reed on it, sort of like a...

Yeah, it, it was a uh, uh, rather long horn, maybe about uh, uh, three feet long, made out of uh, tin. And on the end was a brass reed, soldered to the horn. And on top of that was a wooden mouthpiece. Well, these uh, uh, colored men that drove these uh, wagons would take the mouthpiece off and they, they'd humor that brass reed like a clarinet player humors his uh, uh, clarinet reed to get the various uh, uh, intonation, various pitches. And uh, uh, uh, uh, they most likely are the most gifted people in the world for blues. Uh, so, of course, naturally, uh, his uh, song telling of his uh, approach was uh, uh, the blues. Some one form or another, the blues. Well, of course, uh, uh, I guess maybe just the talented uh, blues players, one end to this business because the, the only ones I can remember played the most uh, beautiful blues you could possibly imagine.
There would have been several of them around and it wasn't just one guy in your neighborhood.

Oh no, no, it wasn't one. They, they were all over town. Yeah. Yeah. And uh, the, uh, I remember these uh, blues as being the most beautiful sound that I could imagine. And uh, they'd play, you could hear them several blocks away and you'd run back shed and get the bottles and be ready for them and climb up on the hub of the wagon. One of these regular wagons, usually uncovered, cheap old battered up wagon with a poor little horse pulling it. And uh, when they'd get there you'd climb up on the hub cap and they'd have a, a box of dirty candy and uh, and little chairs and beds and dolls and toys and things like that. And they'd give you maybe one piece of candy for a few bottles. And stuff like stuff
on the horn or did he sing some too?
No, as I remember everything that he did was on the horn
He didn't have any other cry about

No, no, they had many other colored people with cries, those gorgeous announcers of blackberries that was all such voices the size of a whole cathedral these voices that these colored women have and they'd bring their children along with them and sell blackberries they'd go across the river or go someplace because there was a lot of a wilderness in New Orleans in 1907 and 1908 and they could find blackberries almost any place so they'd load up with blackberries and go around the street selling them and that was an unbelievably musical sound that they had in their blackberries something just beautiful my wife wrote a very cute poem about them once blackberry women and then of course the other the other street criers but those are the two that I remember they were outstanding in my mind the bottle man especially and then the blackberry woman for those enormous gorgeous round juicy voices that they had
and the bottle man didn't sing out then I'd buy baubles or anything like that
no, not that I know of he did all of his talking through his horn
yeah

now they may have had them in other places and of course they they've changed it recently the rag man has been going around with a cowbell of course the bottle man did have a cowbell on his on his horse too yeah but later on I guess anybody took up the the buying and collecting of bottles and maybe some that didn't have the talent to play the horn that way so they depended on the cowbell on the horse horse's neck
can you remember any of the early parades when you were a boy

I remember vaguely a lot of parades yeah and I remember being very impressed with one parade I wouldn't be surprised if it was Papa Lane's band too because there was there was a kid in there playing clarinet and oh it it affected me terribly I at that time I was playing mandolin and violin
or did you ever figure out who this kid was

no no he just passed on the street I remember where I was standing I was standing on the corner of Cronolette and Canal there was a saloon there at that time and I wasn't even on the street I was in the middle of Cronolette because it was roped off then you know so the parade could pass was that Carnival time? yeah it was Carnival Day had to be Carnival Day because it was in the daytime and that was the only parade that they had in the daytime
the Rex Parade

yeah most likely and this kid was playing clarinet and I wonder who he was how old was he? could have been Larry no no I think he was younger than I was at that time this kid and that's the reason I felt sure that I could play a wind instrument when I saw this kid and instead of going crazy for the clarinet when I saw him on clarinet I went crazy for the cornet
you started to tell a minute ago about your first instruments when you started what did you start
well I started on mandolin first my cousin played mandolin and
did you have a teacher?
well he taught me
your cousin
yeah
the older than you

oh yes yes he's 20 years maybe more than that old he was he was a grown practicing lawyer at that time and I got a mandolin I don't remember the inspiration for the mandolin of course in those days every almost everybody had a mandolin or a violin or something like had a string instrument around the house that was the that was the thing later on it got to be ukulele too but the the mandolin didn't ever go out completely well anyway I started on mandolin I took enough lessons from him so I could play by ear and that's all I wanted to do was amuse myself so I fooled with that a little while and later on some kid in the neighborhood had a violin and I went crazy about the violin about how old
were you did you say when you started on mandolin
let's see I must have been about six or seven I guess I was maybe about seven when I started on mandolin
and then on the violin
well that was several years after that may have been nine
did you have violin at home or did you
no I didn't some kid had a violin of course the mandolin and the violin fingering is similar and I fooled on his a little while and I worried my parents for stuff

a violin they weren't any too enthusiastic about it finally they said well if you pass if you get out of this grade we'll give you a violin so I don't know how I ever managed to get out of the grade but I did and I won the violin for that and I took some lessons from a woman by the name of Madame Tuscana I know if anybody ever old enough he has this they'll remember Madame Tuscana Madame maybe it was Madame Tuscana she lived on she had her teaching and also a home on Louisiana Avenue right off of Magazine Street and I will forget taking lessons there she was rather severe too as the old time as well you remember when they used to make you hold a book under your arm so you couldn't raise up your right or your bow arm imagine going over on the g-string with a book over on your arm well that's the way she was and the strong the the the smell of rosin in that in that room was so strong that it smelled like candy it had a candy smell I never smelled of course I was sensitive to everything about bond because I was so wild about it that time so I did the same thing with her I took enough lessons to learn how to play by ear and then I played by ear the rest of the time didn't worry about we played with the kids around the neighborhood Earl Crum who later on got to be the leader of the leader of the owls we used to go to school together and we used to play together he and who else that's about all in the very beginning I believe we were from and I he used to play ukulele and uh I played violin he used to play drum too
to get on with any music other music there were there any other kid bands or any other dance bands that you heard in those days as you were learning yourself

no uh did you ever sneak around there was no such thing as a kid's band except that in the neighborhood you know neighborhood bands not bands but groups would uh would form of course that was a good deal later on you know when when the kids learned how to play yeah pretty well I got up groups like the invincibles that's the group that I played with and then there was the six and seven eights that was the group that Souchon played with and they had those groups in various neighborhoods the invincibles was around uh Napoleon Avenue was a group of boys that lived around Napoleon Avenue
I guess the six and seven eights were around St. Charles Avenue well they were scattered I think they were scattered all over town I mean I think they used to rehearse up that right
stuff years and years later. He played with us in the Invincibles, Bill Clappin was the mandolin
player, you know. You want to go into that Invincibles now,

who else was in the group, and when they... Well, that, of course, that was around 1917 or 1918. No, time of the First World War. Yeah, it was around 1917 or 18 years old. 16 or 1917 or something like that. Did you finish school? Oh, well, I was going off and on to school whenever I could get to it. My father died when I was 15, you know, and that meant I had a young brother seven years old and a mother, and between us two, we kept my brother in school, and I was in and out of school whenever I could get it. Did you get a regular job of some kind then? Yeah, yeah, I got a regular job. I got many of them. I got fired right and left, and I quit a great many of them, too, because I thought they were unreasonable. Oh, the Invincibles? Well, let me see now. Harry Farrar was a piano player, and Frank Farrar, his brother, played violin with me, and Monk Smith, Lester Smith, played guitar, and Earl Crumb played drums. Well, Teddy Farrar played with us sometimes on a ukulele called the Terror Patch, which is a large ukulele. Who else? That was the beginning group, as far as I can see. What kind of music did you play? Oh, we played the jazz tunes, Tiger Rag, and...
Oh, that by ear, and all that. Anybody read much of it?
Ole Miss, nobody read at all that I know of. No, I don't think we'd have anything to do with them if they read. It sounded too conservatory, graduate.
Did you play any jobs, dances, or picnics, or anything?

We played, no, we didn't play for pay, we played for the fun of it. We played at parties here and there, the various people that we knew would ask us over, and they'd dance by us, and then we'd go see girls. Sometimes a group of us would go see girls and play music for them. At the girls' houses and things like that. Once in a while we played for affairs. We played at the St. Charles Hotel for some affair one time. I can't even think of what it was, but I remember that we thought we were cutting up by playing for this big affair. We played free. We didn't get anything for it. We played for the fun of it at Monk Smith's house. We played for the fun of it at Monk Smith's house. He had a music room and we played for the fun of it.
We played for the fun of it at Monk Smith's house. Where did you practice? Any regular times?
Most of the time we played, we didn't call it practice, we just played for the fun of it at Monk Smith's house. He had a music room and we practiced in there and have a grand time with it.
Can you remember any other early bands, for instance, when you first heard Tom Brown? Did you hear him in the old days? No. Or any of the original Dixieland? I never, I tell you. Larry Shields?
No. My impression of the white musician in New Orleans at that time was so low that I wouldn't walk two steps to hear a white musician. The ones that I'd heard had completely disgusted me.
Really? At that time?
Yeah.
Remember that piece?

I just wasn't exposed to the right people. They had them. Tom Brown was playing at that time and Tom Brown could always play well. But I just didn't hear them. The cornet players that I heard around town, I won't mention any names, but they played in the style which we called corny. To this day, people are still playing like that on the west coast. A lot of people are raving about those bands on the west coast. To me, it's still imitation jazz. It's corny. Well, they had many white cornet players that I heard like that. That's the reason I say I wouldn't walk two steps to hear any of the white bands. I had heard when I was conscious of bands around 1917, I had heard that the best, Joe Oliver and the rest of his... I'm not going to call them imitators, but the ones who played in that style, there was only one... Well, there were two styles. There was the style that Fredrik Kepard played, who the group that I played with always considered corny. Now, there's a whole school all over America seems to be built on the Fredrik Kepard style. That's the style that the white men played in New Orleans. But the style that the group that I went with, and I think they were sophisticated in that respect, liked the Joe Oliver style. And so far, it has been proven that they were right. Yeah. There was a vast difference between the Joe Oliver style and the Fredrik Kepard style. Fredrik Kepard had a ricketyk style to our ears and to my ears, he still does. Now, practically all the white men I ever heard in New Orleans played that way. Later on, Dick Mackie played. Now, Dick Mackie played the Joe Oliver style, a very hot, lush style. And I never heard... What's the boy's name I took in Brownlee's band? Can't even think of his name now. Wait a minute. Byers? No, no, no, no. No. Wait a minute. Brownlee's band. Oh, goodness. Wait a minute. The boy who died with consumption, I took his place... Oh, Hardy, sure. Yeah, Emmett Hardy. Emmett Hardy. I never heard Emmett Hardy because I was out of town when Emmett Hardy was playing. Yeah. But he became ill with tuberculosis and when he was laid up, Brownlee heard me on cornet and asked me if I'd play in his band, so I followed him. But I never heard
Emmett Hardy, no. Some people you know rave about how... I have heard nothing but good about him.

I've heard nothing but good. That's right. But not everybody... Yeah. ...says he was great. So he certainly must have been. He must have been. So as I say, I never heard those people. I never heard Dick Mackie until I was grown and Dick Mackie was very good. Now, nobody ever heard of Dick Mackie, you see. And yet he was one of the finest cornet, white cornet players I know that was ever produced in New Orleans. Yeah. The other cornet players were people like Nick LaRocca, you know, I shouldn't mention names. Yeah. I won't go any further. But anyway, to me... Oh, he's dead. He's dead. His feelings. That was a rickety-tick style and to our group, we couldn't take it.
When did you first hear Oliver that you can remember?

Oh, I think it was around 1917 at Tulane Gym. They gave subscription dances every Saturday night at Tulane Gym. And every time they could get him, they got him. Yeah. And they got him for everything else they could get him for too. He had the cream of the crop. He had Kidore on trombone, Johnny Dodge on clarinet. And I don't know whether Baby Dodge was playing drums then. He didn't have Baby Dodge on the drums.
No, I think he used different people like Red Happy, they called him.

Happy Bolton. Yeah. Happy Bolton on drums, who was the greatest drummer I've ever had in my life. Maybe some other people too at times. Yeah, there's no question. I'm quite sure that he'd get up different bands. But he had the same group that could play that really jazz sounding style that we were so crazy about. And to us it sounded like, oh, just something from heaven. I never will get over the sensations I had in the beginning listening to that band. It was just something that I'd never heard before. Although it was reminiscent of those old Negro women singing over the wash tubs and the bottle man and all that, all that Negroid. Am I permitted to use that? Some people frown when you use the word Negroid.
No, no, no, especially.

To me it tells the story pretty well, those Negroid sounds. And Joe Oliver and the people who played in his style all had that particular thing, which to me is a very necessary part of jazz. That bending of notes, stretching of a note, a half tone or maybe more, stretch it as far as you can to get a blues sound. Joe Oliver had that. And he had it to such an extent that I was completely flabbergasted and spellbound. Not only was I, but Monk Smith and Bill Clapinger, we used to spend most of the time standing in front of the band instead of dancing with the pretty girls.
By the way, did you ever go to Tulane or take any work up there?

Yeah, I took some work at Tulane. I never graduated from Tulane. I graduated from Loyola. And I took some work at LSU. I took some master's work at music at LSU. I graduated with a bachelor of music degree from Loyola.
Can you tell us any more about these Saturday night dances? Were they something that fraternities would put on or who?
Oh, no, no. Just certain boys who had a gift for business would hire Tulane Jim and hire the band and charge everybody a dollar to get in. And I guess they made money.
at it I was a little bit too young then around 17 or 18 to to know whether they made money or not the thing that interested me was the pretty girls and and the band that was enough for me
well I'm writing down on the box here about your name Johnny Wiggs when did you change that name and oh you might get in there we only have another minute on

this reel Johnny Wiggs that that that was very recent that is say 17 years ago or something like that I was I'd been teaching school for 15 years and and I had quit teaching music and I felt sort of lost without music and I felt like going back to jazz I hadn't played jazz in maybe 20 years so I went up to see Teddy Fongloo remember he played terror patch with us in the invincibles he was at that time the 1945 he was the sales manager of WSMB so they had another band up there legitimate group of musicians and I said tell you why don't you why don't you give me a job up here give me give my band a job up here I can get a first-class jazz band together he said fine Johnny I'll see if I can't arrange it for you so the poor legitimate band got the skids and we went in and what was the question you asked me now oh wait why'd I change my name yeah well of course I know the school board would frown on me playing stuff stuff He said, fine, Johnny, I'll see if I can't arrange it for you.
So the poor legitimate man got the skids, and we went in. And what was the question you asked me now? Oh, yeah, why did I change my name?

Well, of course, I knew the school board would frown on me playing such lowly music and teaching their pupils, and they wouldn't work politically. Anyway, you know, to have a man playing such indecent music and teaching these saintly children, that were under the...
Okay, go ahead.
What were we talking about?
What about changing your name there when you went on the radio?

Oh, yeah, well, I knew the school board wouldn't like me to continue teaching for them and playing such disreputable music on the air. So I changed my name to Johnny Wiggs, Wiggs being the beginning of Wigington, W-I-G-G-S, beginning of my middle name. And nobody knew I was on there as a school teacher except a few of my friends.
Yeah, because your old Victor records had been made in the 20s. They were...
Yeah, they were under my right name, yeah.

When were they made about? Can you remember a little... Must have been 1926, huh? 1927, was it? We have the dope on it, I guess, probably on the record covers even. I think the Victor company kept records. Who all was on that? Can you remember anything about the date?
You mean the recording?
You don't mean the date of the year? No, I mean the recording section.
Yeah, I remember all about it.
You can tell us a little bit about that.

He was a piano player, a very good piano player, by the name of Diaz, who afterwards went to New York and played commercial music, and I guess he made a lot of money, and I don't blame him for playing commercial music. Hooray for him. He wasn't going to get stuck with this damn fool jazz business, you know, give your soul away and get nothing back. The hell with that. Diaz, who played a beautiful jazz piano, and Monk Hazel was on drums. Elry Mazin on clarinet, much to his disgust, since he was a saxophone player, and swore he couldn't play clarinet, but he played an awful nice clarinet on that record. But I don't think he's played clarinet since then, and he always swore that he could never play the instrument, but he did very well on that record. He was a good saxophone player. Who was the trombone player? Used to be the business manager of the union. What is his name? While we're thinking of him, Nappy Lamar was the guitar player, and that was the first record he ever made, you know, the Nappy Lamar with the Bob Crosby.
Now, let's see,
we've got to remember that trombone player.
You'll think of him in the middle. I can't think he does.
What is his name? Charlie Hartman.
Oh, sure.
Charlie Hartman. Later on was the business manager of the union. And myself on trumpet.
Actually, let me tell you this,

peculiar thing about making records in those days, sometimes they would only make one side, and sometimes they would make two sides. Well, I was lucky enough to have gotten in on the two-side date. But let me tell you, we started making those doggone things at nine o'clock in the morning, and stopped about two or three o'clock in the afternoon.
That long.
And they would take nothing but perfection. There was absolutely, they would take no, not the slightest hint of a flaw.
What building? Where were they made about?
They were made in the warehouse of wire lines. I think it was on Bienville Street, about the 500 block of Bienville Street. They had a warehouse.
Yeah, so it may be where the deck of records is now, a big warehouse. No,
you're thinking of Canal Street.
Yeah, but does it go back that far? It's over two blocks.
Bienville.
That's far over.
This was on Bienville,
yeah. I thought maybe it was just over. No,
this was two blocks, two blocks in the back of Canal Street. Way over that far. Yeah.
Some people made them up there where Deca is now, too, in that big warehouse building.
Yeah, I imagine so. And then they make them in the Gonshaw building. There's a studio there.
Yeah, I remember that.
Which some records have been made.
Seems like you or somebody told us about making them across the street, too, once when you...
Oh, across the street from Wailines? Yeah,
along in that. Yeah,
I tried to get up a group of very fine Negro players, but I made the mistake...
Was it Guy Kelly or somebody?

I'm sure one of them was Guy Kelly and the other one, I can't remember his name. Guy Kelly was a tough, hard to get along with Negro and the other fellow was an easygoing fellow. Both of them were top-notch cornet players, trumpet players.
Would it have been Chris Kelly by any chance? Do you remember? It was Guy Kelly. Was it Chris Kelly of Blue? Oh, I really,
I can't remember the names. I'm not sure. I know this, that they both played in Celestine's band at the same time. I don't know,
I don't know what Celestine was doing. It was Schatz for a while. It was Schatz Madison.

I don't know, but one of them was a mean man and the other one was, one trumpet player was a mean guy and the other one was a very nice fellow. Well, I set them to rehearsing across, Wailines had a sort of a warehouse across the street and without getting any permission because I knew I couldn't get permission for this, I just took it upon myself to take them over there. The Victor recording people were coming down pretty soon and I was trying to rehearse them for a date with the Victor people. and I just took them over there and they got in a fuss with each other, fight with each other and caused such a commotion that the wrap trunk people who were down below them rang up Wailines and wanted to know what all that commotion was. So Wailines rang down to the band incident department and I don't know how I got the information but I got it, I got it quick enough to go over there and get that band out of there before I got myself in trouble and that was the end of an awful good record date because there were two top notch trumpet players and a fine clarinet player and trombone and piano. I don't think I had the whole band together because it's easy enough to put in a bass and a drum, you know, but that was the end of that recording date. Oh and we had a, we had a date lined up which could have been very good. I'll tell you about this date but I won't mention the name of the trombone player who got to be very famous. Snoozer Quinn, I was going to use, it was another Victor date. I was going to use Snoozer Quinn on guitar and Siegfried Christensen on piano and Eddie Miller on clarinet and I was going to play cornet and there was a trombone player who was playing around town then. Well, we rehearsed that were going to be original numbers. Well, we rehearsed and the trombone player couldn't learn it the first day. So we rehearsed another time and he couldn't learn it the next day. He couldn't, he just couldn't learn the thing. So that was the end of that. I just gave up in disappointment. But what a pity to have lost that. And at that time
Snoozer, of course,

I was about to say at that time Snoozer had never been recorded but Snoozer hadn't been recorded. But Snoozer has never been recorded except the 12 sides that I have of his. They've never been released. The 12 sides that I have have never been released yet.
The four sides are all that came out.
Yeah, I put out four sides myself.
Remember that business in the paper about four or five months ago? Did you see that when people, somebody mentioned Snoozer Quinn?
Oh, Bing Crosby, the great almighty God
Bing Crosby wanted to know
something about Snoozer Quinn and everybody fell on their face trying to get information out to Bing Crosby. What happened to Snoozer Quinn? He was dead even.
Yeah, they didn't even know he was dead. Oh, no, no.
Very few people knew he was dead.

Let's see, while we're talking about recording dates, can you tell us anything about Tony Parente's dates? They were the Colombias, weren't they? Are Victor's? Wait a minute, let me think. I believe it was
either OK or Colombia. I can't remember.
Some were on Victor and some are Colombias, mostly.
Well, I mean, the date I was on, I don't know anything at all about the others.
Were you only on one date? Yeah, I was only on
one record, two sides, yeah.
Two sides.
Yeah. One was called In the Dungeon and the other was when you and I were pals. And on that date there was Tony and Alice Stratigas, I believe, on trombone.
That reminds me, you're on a record he made on Vocalion, is that right? Stratigas?
Yeah, yeah.
So I never could find it, never did find it.

I have one. I have a beat up one. Myself, I've been looking for a good copy for years. I've never been able to find it. Oh, yeah.

B. Palmer, yeah. Well, as I say, Bix and Trombaugh and Snoozer were over at her house. Some of the Whiteman boys, the jazz department of Whiteman, was over at B. Palmer's house one Sunday afternoon, and they were playing around, and first thing you know, B. Palmer caught a whiff of this guitar, you know? And she listened to him a little while, and she finally said to Bix and Trombaugh, I know what you fellas can do. Could I get a little bit of this guitar by himself and see what he sounds like? And so they stopped playing, and Snoozer took over, and he really took over. And I have in writing, or in Blackstone has in writing, an answer to this article I wrote in his magazine, from B. Palmer, saying that every word of it was true, said that she was just completely knocked out of her mind when she heard Snoozer Quinn. Now here's the other one about the Columbia. Snoozer can't remember whether it was Columbia or not, but anyway, they were playing, they were playing maybe for the fun of it somewhere. You know how those fellas were always with the instruments, Bix and Trombaugh and Snoozer and people like that. And they were playing for the fun of it, and Snoozer began humming along with his stuff, and he was humming the same licks that he was playing on guitar. So Trombaugh, always a late, he's a very late guy, you know, said, gee whiz, let's get this on wax right away. So they went up to some studio, and Snoozer can't remember what it was, he said, I think it was Columbia. And they made some records, and of all things, singing the blues was one of them. And for some reason, they never did get out. Just like everything that Snoozer recorded was not released. He recorded a dozen sides for Victor, and I bet you $10 they don't have one master left. They were never released.
With Whiteman?
No, by himself, by himself.
By himself.
Right after I made those Victor records, I told Victor people about him. I said, you better get this guy. So they got a whole bunch of stuff by him, see?
Yeah, in those days.

Not considered commercial, couldn't release it. Same thing happened in Houston with Columbia. Took a whole bunch of his tunes, never released. When he was with Whiteman, you never could hear him. They never would give him a pickup, you know, so he could get on records. He recorded with this moron, Jimmy Davis, who is called the governor of Louisiana. And Jimmy Davis starts singing the minute the needle was dropped on the wax and stopped singing when the thing got through. And you couldn't hear hardly one note of Snoozer Quinn.
Remember the name of the song? I didn't know he was with Jimmy Davis.
Yeah, he made some things with Jimmy Davis. No, Orrin Blackstone had them. I wouldn't want her. I wouldn't want her. Orrin Blackstone had the records.
They're not repending enough.
I wouldn't. Oh, they're vile.
I still see some of the Jimmy Davis. I picked up a couple of them. I don't know which ones or whose would be on.

You wouldn't be able to tell he was on them, no, any more than with Whiteman. You can't hear a word. Yeah. I never heard a man hog a thing like Jimmy Davis did. Those things. I mean, you know, most people would give a man like Snoozer a solo because there's a sparkling, terrific beauty there, you see. But no, God Almighty, the man starts singing when the needle drops to cut the record and stops when the record's over.
No introduction or anything.
Boy, what is that, a needle hog or a groove hog, huh? Oh, thank God he can do something, hog a record, huh? He sure can't run a state. And I hope that gets to his ears.
Wouldn't worry him.
No, he's had so many. Yeah, yeah, he's had so many things.
Got his money. That's all he wants.

Stupid moron. The whole country's run by stupid morons. He's not the only one. No, but... You can't get to be an elected official in this country without being a stupid moron. You'd have to be a stupid moron to run.
I'm afraid so. Well, let's see. Is there anything else about the New Orleans jazz?
Anything you want to say?
Anything else about the New Orleans style of playing or anything about organizing bands or the way you like... What do you think is a good band?
I mean, the right style to play
or anything remotes?

I like a band to be rehearsed. You can still get that good new audience sound with a band that knows what it's doing. I just don't like to play like they play down here. Now, when I say down here, I've only been living here for 63 years, you see, since the day I was born, except when I left town for a few years. But I don't like the way they play down here. Unless I was playing with a good Negro rhythm section, you see, then you can do no wrong. But here, where you're walking on a tightrope with a rhythm section that's going to upset you any two seconds, I want a band well rehearsed. And you can't get them well rehearsed. Not only that, you can't get anybody in New Orleans... Really, nobody in New Orleans loves jazz. That's the whole truth of it. I mean, no... I say nobody. I mean no white jazz musicians like jazz. Because if they like jazz, they'd like to get together and play. But one of them has this reason for not playing. I only play when I get paid. The other can't play because somebody brings his babies over to their house. And another one can't play because he's always got jobs. And another one can't play because he's got to deliver babies all the time. And there's always a reason. Now, all over the country, you can get rarities such as string instruments that will be delighted to get together and play once a week. Think of Mencken's group and your group to get together on strings. All over the country, you find people that love music enough so that they want to get together once a week. For 17 years, I've been trying to get a group together that would play once a week just for the love of jazz. So I finally gave up last year. It just is not possible. So my conclusion is that nobody, no white man that can play jazz in this town really loves it. Because if he loved it, he'd love to play it.

Oh, one other question I was going to ask about different tunes. Do you have any idea on should you be able to play any kind of a pop commercial Tin Pan Alley tune? Or do you like some of the old Dixieland favorites? Are there blues? Or what kind of numbers are best for a jazz band? Or what do you enjoy playing? Or what do you think they should play?

Oh, well, I think some numbers out of each category. Are good. Numbers, of course, like rumbas and things like that are kind of hard to do much with. But ordinarily, well, the pieces that have stuck, like My Blue Heaven and Out of the Popular Group, are always good. And Indiana, my home in Indiana, those stick all the time. I mean, you can't get rid of them. And those are popular. Of course, most of the jazz tunes lend themselves to jazz naturally.
Yeah.
The pieces that I love most of all are the old Negro sort of spirituals. You know, like, in so long since I've played, I can't even think of the name. Yeah.
What is it? Just Closer Walk.
Closer Walk with E. And Pattern on the Floor.
Around the Riverside.

Somewhere around the hill. Yeah. Yeah. And Old Miss. Old Miss. Yeah. I love that tune. The way Joe Oliver used to play it up in Tulane Gym. He just played the chorus. He didn't play the whole arrangement, which, by the way, is terrific. The whole arrangement is fine.
It was always in Bugle Call Rag. They used it as a special, like, trio section.
Well, I, you know, you know who Face put it on a record? I did with Tony Perranti. We played, we got a tune which was a blues.
Yeah.
And we ran.
Ole Miss into it. In the dungeon. That was the first time.

They do that sometimes with Bugle Call up north. They thought it was part of Bugle Call. You might make a few remarks about some of the tunes that you've written. The Congo Square. That was your tune, wasn't it?
Yeah, Congo Square.
What are some of the others? I can't think of all of them now.
Let me see.
King Zulu Parade.
Gallatin Street Grind. Shepin Tua Joys. Postman's Lament. Well, this thing that Al Rose recorded, he insisted on me using the title Pelican Panic.
Was it something like Canal and Royal?
Oh, yeah. There was a Canal and Royal. And a, there's a, oh goodness, I can't think of them.

I might ask about how you write them. I think we have a couple of sketches that you gave us once that are in the Tulane Library. Or, you know, the little lead sheets and all. Or, how much of that do you write out? Do you write, I forget now, have you had any piano parts written out too? Or, when you copyright them, what do you do?
I just copyright a lead sheet. Just the lead sheet. Most of the time. Sometimes I send a piano part with, but the piano part will be the lead with chords, so it's nothing but a lead sheet.
Yeah.

Because I don't, naturally I'm not going to write a piano part, I'm just going to write the lead with, for the piano player. Yeah. Well, I did most of that arranging at my desk at Warren Easton High School, on the school
board side.
I was at WSMB when I arranged most of those things for my band, you see. Yeah. And, uh.

We have about two or three more minutes on here. Any other remarks that you want to make in parting? We can stop at any time. We don't have to fill it up. I can't think of anything. Sorry to run out of questions.
Unless you can stimulate some thought with me.

You mentioned once before that the three great musicians, Snoozer of course we were talking about, and Louie and Bix, you didn't mention Joe Oliver. At other times you've told me you thought Joe Oliver had something that Louie never quite got. We all know Louie, he's wonderful. I'm trying to knock in.

Yeah, I think, well of course Louie doesn't have much resemblance to Joe Oliver anymore, although I think he's, uh, contrary to most, uh, died in the world jazz people, I think he's a very great performer, jazz performer today. He just hasn't been in good settings. But Joe Oliver had a dirty tone, which Louie almost got to perfection when Louie first hit New York. Of course Louie, uh, breathed on, on everything that Joe Oliver did, you know? Yeah. I mean, he studied Joe Oliver as close as a person could ever study anybody. Uh, Joe Oliver had, had that dirty tone, which, uh, which jazz people have come to love so much. Uh, and, uh, I can't say that, that, that, uh, that Louie missed it much. Uh, like, uh, like the records of Everybody Loves My Baby and, uh, and, yeah, those Clarence Williams records. I don't think Louie was very far away from that dirty tone at that time. Since then, of course, he's gotten a good way away from it, yeah. But it takes too much of a person's lip to play like that. It's a, oh, it's a unbelievable, uh, uh, uh, strain on your lip. You see, Joe Oliver played with a mute in his hand. Uh, the mute was halfway in his bell. And right there is a strain on your lip. You're not holding the cornet, uh, with, with the ease that you should hold it, you see? And, uh, uh, the way he worked his hand in and out of there, uh, to help bend those notes, and the dirty sound he got, well, the, the nearest thing I've ever heard was Louie to that. Uh, as I, as I told you before, Joe used to really knock me out of my mind up at Tulane Gym. Yeah. Oh, one cute thing I'd like to tell you about, uh, Joe Oliver. Uh, he was a very supercilious Negro, you know? He knew what he had. He was, uh, he was a big boy in, in, in music in New Orleans. Yeah. He had all the jobs tied up, you see? And he took nothing from nobody. So sometimes, uh, he'd play, uh, after a tune was over, somebody would come up and ask him, uh, what was that tune you played last? And he, he'd say, uh, who struck John? No matter what it was, you know? Yeah. If it was a nice little girl who would ask him, or a boy or somebody, he cared nothing for none of them, you know? Yeah. Another funny thing he used to do, he had a, he had skin over his eyes, I don't know what you, over one eye. And his eye was, uh, I don't know whether they call it cataract or not, but the skin was growing over his eye, one eye. And that eye was cocked, too. It was looking out towards the left, you see? Yeah. Well, he, he always had a brown derby. And he put his brown derby when he was playing over there, he used it for, uh, for a mute, too, sometimes, you know? He used, uh, he, uh, put that over his good eye and he'd stare out into space over to the left with that cock eye, you know? He was a real sassy nigga, I'm telling you. Cute as hell. Mean, too, boy. He was, he was really mean, yeah. He was, uh, yes, sir. It sure was fun to watch that guy. I mean, he had that band under control, too, boy. He was the boss. He was the boss. Yes, sir.

One thing I plan to ask you, if there's anything you can tell us about Tom Brown, since we never got to talk to him, or any of our Tulane tapes. I know you played with him, recorded with him a lot. Any remarks about him?

Yeah, well, Tom Brown, uh, was a very interesting person to watch. He was different from anybody, and he could, uh, he could analyze what you were talking about immediately, and he had a hair, uh, trigger temper, you know? Yeah. If he didn't like it, boy, you were gonna get it right away. That's right. And, uh, he was very different from Steve. Steve Brown, who I think is the greatest white bass player I've ever heard in my life. Oh, just out of the world, that marvelous bass player. Too bad those kind of people, those kind of white rhythm people can't stay in the audience here. Yeah. But we have to have piccolo players on bass fiddle here, you know?
Yeah.

Uh, well, anyway, uh, Tom, uh, had a hair-trigger temper, and he just didn't take anything from anybody. But he, he was a, he was a cute guy to be with. Yeah. And, oh, I tell you, we, to, to, to play with him, sometimes, sometimes he'd look way back.
